subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES-IMMEDIATE PAYMENT OF $100 MILLION TO WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the NDP referred to himself as a "city feller" and explained that he did not wish to appear to be misrepresenting himself as an expert on farming. Of course I, too, have to confess that when it comes to the complexities of making a crop grow, I am strictly an amateur, although I should point out, with some degree of reality, I have had some modest success as a gardener. While the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) draws the line at calling himself a "city feller", I might be inclined to go a little bit further and describe myself as a bluenose by birth with a green thumb by practice.
Like the leader of the NDP, I feel it is imperative that all Canadians in all walks of life take an active and concerned interest in the affairs of Canadian agriculture today, not only from an economic point of view but from a human point of view as well. I have tried to follow what I think is good advice in this regard. I had the good fortune of growing up in a small town which was the centre of an agricultural community. I was well aware from the start of the contributions that farmers make to the general community life, the general provincial life and the general national life. Unfortunately, I have also been able to follow rather closely the many problems that have developed throughout the years, including problems of adjustment.
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers
In my original part of Canada, the Atlantic provinces, there were problems which one could follow through Quebec, Ontario and into the west. There has been a tendency on the part of this government to write off the farm. It might not be strictly accurate to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as asking: "Why should I sell your wheat", but this was pretty indicative of the attitude displayed in the west, and that cannot be denied.
I have had an opportunity to visit some farms in the west and I was very struck by the qualities of these people, their capacities and their problems. I had the opportunity of living on one farm for a while last September. I was very struck by three aspects. First, there was a very strong feeling on the part of the farmer for his farm. You could almost feel the attachment between that farmer and his farm. Secondly, I was impressed by the extent of the efforts which had been made by that farmer and other farmers in his area-and this is substantially a grain farming area-to diversify. I know many people in the east think that the western farmer simply grows wheat and expects it to be sold. It was an eye-opener to me to realize the extent of the diversification which is taking place, even on what are basically grain farms in the west. I had an opportunity to visit an elevator there. I was shown samples of crops which had been delivered up until a couple of years ago. I saw the great range of crops now being delivered to that elevator. I believe it is very important that people in the eastern part of Canada realize the extent to which the western farmer has attempted to diversify and the extent to which he has worked to try to solve his own problems.
The third thing which impressed me-and this obviously was an exceedingly well-run operation in respect of which great efforts were made toward diversification- was the size of the investment in the farm. The farmer showed me his accounts, as audited by the people in the minister's own Department of Agriculture. The size of the investment was striking. It was very clear that this man was living on the depreciation of his equipment. He was hanging on. I could not help but ask myself how long this situation could continue. I believe this was a typical example of an excellently run farm. I could not help but wonder how much more difficult it must be on smaller farms which are not in as fortunate a position. Here, we had a substantial operation, fierce determination, hard work, a love of the soil and a tremendous pride. I could not help but think how important the person who operates such a farm is to Canada.
I knew something about farmers in the east. I had not had such close contact with farmers in the west before. I realized how much these people mean to Canada, how terrible it would be if they went under and how important it is that they be helped, not in the sense of things being made easy-that is not what they expect-but in the sense of being assisted so that they are able to work out their problems. We have heard references to figures in this House today, and at other times, concerning the drop in net farm income in the west. This does not apply

June 8, 1971
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers merely to the west, although the difficulty there is perhaps more striking than in the rest of the country. What we must bear in mind is that this drop in income does not affect only the farming economy. As the minister knows, it also affects the whole economy of the west and the rest of the country. It affects the suppliers, the merchants and the whole basis of our economy. It is important to bear in mind that we are really talking about a subtantial segment of the whole economy. The farmers have been having a bad time with increasing debts and with an inadequate program as well as a very inadequate attitude on the part of the government.
This is not the time to talk about the adequacy of the government's programs and the switch from a storage support program to an inadequate grain stabilization program. But it is the time to emphasize the importance of helping farmers and encouraging them to move ahead. This is the reason I wished to take part in this debate today and to say something as fiercely as I can. Clearly, the passing of this motion today would of course, in a sense, simply be a palliative. Certainly, it would not really solve anything. I do not pretend that the payment of $100 million to the farmers would in itself solve their problems, although I believe it would give them a real lift. I want to emphasize the need for a different and wholehearted approach rather than the hesitant approach to farming and agricultural policies this government has adopted. What is shocking and revolting to me is that after three years under the present government, years in which there have been no major natural catastrophes, we are being forced to consider a motion of this kind in this House.
This all points up the fact that this government in itself is a catastrophe from the point of view of the worker, the businessman, the hundreds of thousands of unemployed who are walking our streets and the farmer. With this government in the saddle there is no need of a natural disaster. It seems to carry its own disasters with it wherever it goes. That is why there is a need for this motion or one like it. After three years of rule, or rather misrule, this government has dragged down agriculture just as it has dragged down the economy as a whole. Three years ago promises were made of a just society and of prosperity ahead. Just like other people in Canada-the city dweller, the small businessman and all others who made the mistake of believing the slogans or who even if they did not believe them were forced to live with them in any event-the farmers have been losing their confidence in a government which has clearly lost its way. This is not confined to western farmers. This is a feeling which unites farmers from the east and from the *west.
Certainly, there has not been unanimity among farmers. Certainly there are differences between regions and between producers of various kinds of farm produce. But one reason for these problems surely is the failure of this government, after three years, to come up with any sort of arrangement that is acceptable to the agriculturalists and the livestock producers of this country.

speechtext:
They seem to be in trouble over there, Mr. Speaker. I do not know whether it is their consciences we are hearing from now. Instead, the solution of this government has been to divide, the better to rule; to divide the farmers among themselves and to divide them from the men and women who live in the cities and who curse the high cost of living, often unfairly blaming the producers of the foods they are buying. The guiding principles of the government in relation to agriculture are expressed time and time again in terms such as "viability" and "rationalization". It is bad enough that their jargon is based on economic pessimism. But it is infinitely worse that this kind of lingo totally ignores any humanistic approach to agriculture as a way of life.
Surely, the report of the government's task force on agriculture is one of the most pessimistic pieces of literature ever authored. It should have been entitled "grim expectations". I think the Minister of Agriculture might very well take a look to the south of him; he might take a look at the attitude of the United States government towards agriculture and its determination to sell. I think the effort on the part of this government to get out and sell has been very limited compared to the efforts of the United States. The record of the United States indicates that there is an opportunity for success if the government, when it has things to be sold, would only get at it.
We cannot let the government get away with this sort of thing any longer. We have to point out to the men and women who are suffering from economic recession in the cities that the farmer, too, is suffering. The point cannot be made too often. The policy of the government for the cities and towns has been, of course, to slow down the economy. In the country, on the other hand, it is rather difficult, even for this government, to slow down the growing season, so it has just decided to weed out the farmer instead.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) denies that the government intends to drive people off the farms, whether or not they are efficient. All I can say is that if he does not intend to do this, he had better look pretty quickly at the policies that he is pursuing because that is the effect that these policies are having. If that is not the intention of the present government, then what we have is just another example of sheer incompetence and blundering by this government.

June 8, 1971

off the farms. Will it kindly tell us what it is trying to do? There is no evidence of a clear policy leading in any direction. Once again, in the field of agricultural production, we have a government that seems to be proceeding without a plan but trusting blindly to luck. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES-IMMEDIATE PAYMENT OF $100 MILLION TO WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the agricultural problem is not settled, as it is discussed even in Parliament on many occasions with a view to helping the government to the greatest extent possible in finding the proper solutions to promote the agricultural industry, not only in one area but all over the country.
I feel that the motion before the House shows that a really difficult situation exists particularly as regards the western farmers. However, the intention of the sponsor of this motion was to emphasize a situation which may be to the disadvantage of the eastern farmers. The mover has therefore proposed as a solution that the farmers be granted an amount of at least $100 million over and above the farm assistance programs.
In taking part in the debate on the motion now before the House, I should like, once again, to suggest to the government that its agricultural policy is not entirely fair to farmers, and that the farmers' net income is not high enough to enable them to get their fair share of the national product. I do not mean by this that the government is not doing anything, that the whole of his policy is to be condemned, but that not enough is done to give farmers, who devote their life to tilling the soil so as to feed mankind, a chance equal to that of citizens who work at other activities of the Canadian economy.
I should like, in this debate, to suggest some solutions which may perhaps seem ridiculous, because some will feel that the time has not come to put them into practice, but, frankly, I consider that means must be taken, other than the present ones, to solve the problem.
In the summer of 1970, after having visited several areas in the Prairie provinces, and after having talked with many farmers, I finally understood that several of them are in very difficult financial circumstances. They have a hard time finding help for the farm; this forces them to get more equipment, of the most modem and expensive type, which plays havoc with their budget and increases the cost of production.
During my trip, I noticed some modern equipment in farm yards, and while speaking with the farmers, found out that they had to use more modem means to do their work at a reasonable cost, because they found it next to impossible to get farm hands.
The farmer, who for that matter is not responsible for price increases, is nevertheless penalized for he must pay a higher interest on his loans. He must also pay more and
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers more for the components of his production, without getting more for his products. Therefore the cost-price squeeze becomes tighter, which contributes to make life more and more difficult.
On the matter of interest, I am convinced that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) will announce in due course a reduction of interest rates. I would welcome such news. The opinions we voiced when interest rates were raised have finally been heeded. Interest rates must be lowered even further. This will automatically help farmers to operate at lower cost.
There are farm problems in all Canadian provinces. That is why the provincial and federal governments must co-operate fully so that Canadian agriculture may flourish as much as possible.
There is a grain surplus in the prairies and in order to reduce stocks on hand, the government promotes pork meat production, which results in competition between eastern and western farmers, in short by pitting them one against the other.
As for me, I cannot blame the western farmer who finds himself unable to sell the grain stored on his farm and raises hogs to use up his production. But when that production appears on the market, there is a clash between western breeders and farmers because the latter cannot produce on a competitive level. In fact eastern pork producers are not in position to match the low costs posted by western producers since even with current subsidies for feed grain transportation-which are not high enough-the eastern producer is producing with a disadvantage of $3 to $5 per hog. The purpose of the current government policy is therefore to pit the regions one against the other and this is unfortunate.
Let us see now what is going on in the field of eggs and broilers where, because of farm surpluses which in fact are not actual surpluses, underconsumption prevails. This situation is described in the reports of the Economic Council, so this is not something I dreamed up. The Council stated that many Canadians have inadequate income and are underfed. Let us call a spade a spade. Instead of mentioning surpluses we should speak of underconsumption. In fact a great many families are living in privation because they cannot buy what they actually need. I do not mean luxury but things essential to life.
We are currently witnessing a continued decrease in the purchasing power of low income families. In fact, in Quebec, it has been found that by virtue of the implementation and the interpretation of the new legislation which was enacted November 1 and which permits the state to help needy people, the level of these pensions is generally lower. I receive many letters from people who complain, most often rightly, that their pension has decreased. Moreover the unemployment rate keeps rising, which results in a reduction of the purchasing power of low income people.
I do not think that the pensioners and the unemployed have spent $30 per week to feed their families, as

June 8, 1971
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers indicated in a report from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which I should like to quote in part:

In 1969, each Canadian family spent $28.80 per week for food, as shown by an inquiry carried out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
The largest amount ($31.70 per week) was spent in the urban centres of the province of Quebec, and the lowest ($21.40) in the rural areas of the Prairie provinces.
According to a per capita computation, the highest figure ($7.40 per week) for the rural sector was found in British Columbia, and the lowest ($6.03 per person) in the Atlantic provinces.
Such data prove that consumption is directly linked to economic conditions, in other words, to the take-home pay, and the family spends more or less accordingly. I now resume the quotation:
As for the cities, Ontario ranks first ($8.83 per person) whereas the Atlantic provinces come last on the list ($7.31 per week).
This is the first such survey made by DBS for the past twenty years-
So, this is not new.
Every dollar spent on food can be broken down as follows:
Red meat, poultry and fish, 28 cents; fruits and vegetables, 13 cents; cereals, bakery and confectionery products, 10 cents; dairy products (including butter), 13 cents; food oils and other fats, 2 cents; eggs, 3 cents; frozen foods, 1 cent; miscellaneous, 13 cents; foods prepared, bought and eaten outside home, including board, 17 cents.
This means that in order to bring consumption to the required level, we should increase income in a different way than it has been done to date. We shall have to use new methods if we are to meet this objective and put the Canadian economy back on its feet, so that all Canadians be treated in a fair way.
And to increase the farmer's income, the greater part of our domestic market would first have to be reclaimed in order to dispose of our farm products. This would become possible in part by providing for a direct increase in consumer purchasing power, and for a guaranteed minimum income at all times during the year. Such steps would help maintain a better economic balance and would result in a more regular consumption on Canadian products, whether they be foodstuffs or anything else.
This guaranteed minimum income should also be available to farmers. Then, whatever the prices, the rural people would also be assured of a guaranteed minimum income and instead of having to cope with major difficulties which get worse from year to year, they would at least hopefully look to a guaranteed minimum income.
For this guaranteed minimum income to be paid, we would have to do the opposite of what is now being done when social benefits are allowed to the various classes of our society. When people are taxed, they find themselves in a difficult situation. Indeed, two years ago when the government moved to boost old age pensions, we did expect a new levy to cover the costs involved. We were in a very embarrassing position. We were in favour of higher pensions for old people but, on the other hand, we did not want any new taxes or an increase in those already existing.
Lest we be accused of being against old people, we had to accept new taxes. That is why, in my view, we should find new formulas to finance the assistance programs based on the production potential of Canada.
If our country is unable to produce enough goods to meet the demand of Canadians, it would be useless to pass social measures providing for higher income if Canadians were unable to purchase the goods they hope to get in order to satisfy their needs.
In order to meet the costs of this guaranteed income, the government should resort to the Bank of Canada. There will again be people to say: The Creditistes are always talking about the Bank of Canada. Indeed they do and they are going to talk about it. The government talks about taxes and we put up with that! Let us do the same then when we honestly advocate reforms. We have to use the Bank of Canada. We use it to other ends. Why should we not use it to such noble ends as the solution of the farmers' problem, by giving them an opportunity of selling their products and by increasing the income of the consumers in a logic and fair proportion?
The Bank of Canada would then be authorized to issue new credits as national production, based on the work of Canadians, increases. Without production, there would be no new credits!
In any event, there would surely be an increase in purchasing power, and this recall of new credits would have to be done through taxation when production drops, in order to strike a balance as much as possible between production and consumption.
This has long been the objective of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and of economists: to try to strike a balance between production and consumption so that the Canadian economy will be sound and people, in all sectors, well-off.
It is very important to make a careful appraisal of the total cost and of the advantages of a new welfare and guaranteed income policy, even from the standpoint of agriculture, because it is in that area that the voice of those who are really in need is less often and less loudly heard.
The motion now before the House suggests that the government should pay out $100,000,000 in subsidies, without conditions, and in addition to other farm assistance programs. This may seem a large amount but if it is spread over the last ten years when farmers were having problems, it only represents $10,000,000 a year.
In concluding my remarks, I wish to point out to the government that Canada is one of those countries which are not very generous toward agriculture. The United States are doing much more for their farmers and the Common Market countries are getting more liberal with their money, in fact, $3 billion were voted by them for farm assistance.
I therefore urge the government to do more for farmers so that they will cease to be victims of an obsolete system and will get their just share of the national income.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to take part in this debate on a subject very close and dear to my heart, life in the rural communities of Canada as we presently know it. The motion before the House condemns the agricultural policies of the government which have severely reduced the income of western farmers and calls on the government to consider the advisability of an immediate payout to them of $100 million.
This motion was moved by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis). I am pleased to see the NDP supporting the concept of acreage payments. I do not want to be political, yet I can remember that when the government of the day in 1959 proposed acreage payments, the hon. member's group ridiculed the idea. The leader of that party said the amount to be paid was peanuts. Let me say quickly, Mr. Speaker, and one need not be a mathematician to arrive at this conclusion, that $40 million in 1959 about equals $100 million in 1970 if one takes into consideration the effects of inflation. In any event, it is pleasant to see the NDP supporting acreage payments, a concept well known to and firmly accepted by western Canada. It is regrettable that the government has tied its proposal regarding the $100 million payout to the provisions of Bill C-244. I do not
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers believe that Bill C-244 mentions, nor did the minister in charge of the Wheat Board in the statement made on October 29 mention, that $100 million.

It is terrible that the government has to offer a bribe of $100 million in order to get a piece of legislation accepted. Surely, if the legislation has merit it should stand on its own feet.
May I deal with another aspect of this motion, an aspect very dear to my heart, that relating to our present day rural communities. I have before me a copy of the Manitoba Co-Operator of May 20, 1971. An article in it refers to the "Adjustment Program For Canada's Farms". It reads in part:
Details of the proposed agricultural adjustment or development policy of the federal government have been revealed in a paper prepared by the Canada Department of Agriculture. The paper said the federal cabinet has given approval in principle for the development and operation of a set of adjustment policies and programs of the general type outlined in the 20-page document.
The article goes on to outline these policies, and states that they come under three major headings:
-the first main group of policies will be designed to improve the ability of farm people to make adjustments required to increase the attainments of their personal goals.
Under the plan the individual farmer and his family would be provided with information and counselling services-
That is the first of these policies. The article continues:
A second sub-group of policies is designed to increase the mobility of land resources to facilitate outmigration of people from agriculture and the consolidation of farms within agriculture.
Some time ago the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, who is not present in the House, rose with all the indignation he could muster when we, in the opposition, charged the government with attempting to put farmers off the land. That was not the case at all, he said. If that is so, why has the program outlined in the 20-page document referred to been approved, and what is the meaning of "policies... designed to increase the mobility of land resources to facilitate outmigration of people from agriculture". If those words do not mean that the government wishes to do away with small family farms, I do not know what they mean. You know, the more I read

I continue quoting:
A third sub-group would increase the availability and control of capital through various forms of credit and through various contractual arrangements used in the acquisition and control of land and other capital.
So power hungry is this government that it wants to control not only capital, but land as well. I hope the minister will not try to say that the government does not want to drive the owner of the family farm out of farming.
The article continues:
It was understood that planners in the agriculture department have been told that the adjustment in Canadian agriculture must take place within this generation, or within 15 years.
So, the small farmer is given 15 years to live, then he must move to the city and go on welfare. What will happen to all the small communities, to the small grocers and the curling rinks and to all the people who live in small communities? Fifteen years is all those people have been given. I will not read all the article, but this part reads:
One spokesman for the federal department said the "utopian condition" would be to reduce the farm population in Canada to 150,000 people by the final stage, but it was realized that this might not be achievable.
Well, they are holding out a 10 per cent chance for the small farmer to survive; that's mighty big of them. I continue quoting the article:
The paper sees three major thrusts within Canadian agricultural policy.

We know all about that.

speechtext:
I can read it over again. The present government has created a need for credit facilities because they have increased the interest rate from 5 per cent to 8 per cent on loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation. They are not doing much for the prospective buyers of land, either. The article continues:
Authority (for the government) to enter the market directly to purchase and resell farms as the needs arise.
The bureaucrat is moving into the real estate business. I should not be warning the small farmers, I should be warning the real estate men across this country that they will have opposition. The government is going to move in. It has the ultimate power to buy and sell land. The government is going to collect it all because they are going to be marketing the farmers' products under this two-headed monster that is responsible for agricultural policy today. If one reads this complete article, he will realize where we are headed. I quote:
The second set of programs is comprised of:
A rural counselling service required to assist the farmer and his family make the basic decision-

June 8, 1971

A farm management service-
An agricultural adjustment information system-
I wonder whether this system will come under Information Canada which is going to set up stores across Canada. One can clearly see the bureaucratic drive going forward in the Department of Agriculture. One has to really study that. What are they attempting to gain by it?
We hear a great deal of discussion today about the standard of living. Does it really satisfy the people? We hear discussions about the quality of life. In my opinion, the quality of life is highest on the small farms across Canada. It should be the goal of politicians to strive to give people a high quality of life. They should encourage the small farmer to stay on the farm and not drive him into the city. I will tell you why I believe that.
In order to enjoy a high quality of life, one must reach some degree of contentment with himself and his community. He must have peace of mind and the knowledge that the food and shelter are his and will be there. He can acquire that on a small farm. In order to reach that contentment, he must have the satisfaction that he is making a meaningful contribution to his family, community and country. He can do this most readily in the agricultural rural community. Above all, in order to have contentment, he must have a sense of security and freedom. This can be most readily acquired in a rural community or on a small farm.
What is happening in other segments of our society? A fear is developing. A headline in this morning's Gazette refers to the inroads of the mafia. If we look at the crime that is developing in our major cities, we see that it is difficult for an individual to reach a degree of certainty. It is not good enough to merely lock the door. In nine out of 10 homes in rural communities across Canada, they do not bother to lock their doors at night. Ninety-nine out of 100 farms are not locked at night. They have a sense of security on the farm. The cities are reaching a point where they cannot offer the same high quality of life.
Other things happen to the environment when men are grouped too closely together. There is a high crime rate. Frustration builds up from a lack of contentment. It drives people to violence and crime. What about the concern for the pollution of our air, water and land? The concentration of the automobiles in major cities contributes something like 62 per cent to the air pollution. This is not the case in the rural communities which the government is deliberately attempting to destroy with a plan that is set out in a 20 page document which they are trying to sell to the provinces. This program is deliberately destroying the highest quality of life that Canadians can hope to enjoy. What about pollution of our land and water? When men are grouped together in close confinement, it is very difficult and costly to maintain a high quality of life.
Let us take a quick look at what we really want to do. Above all, we want to build our country. We also want to protect our past. If you take an extreme example, a farmer realizes that he has inherited his land from somebody who farmed it before him and he must protect it
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers for somebody who will follow. He develops a love for the past and a deep sense of protection of the environment for those who will follow. This feeling is not acquired in the city. In the city, people acquire a sense of frustration which leads them to knock down huge buildings to get them out of the way so that the air will be pure and clear. It is different in the rural areas. The farmer has a deep desire to protect the land which he has acquired. He believes he has to protect it for his life, family, community and country. This is the type of country he wants. We want a person to enjoy a high quality of life. We want him to have a sense of freedom.
If we follow this adjustment program which the government has laid down in this 20 page document, will these people still have a sense of freedom? The government will help these people decide whether they go left, right or in the middle. I do not mean that in a political sense. There are three choices. The government will help an individual make a decision. As far as the government is concerned, that will be his first and last decision. He will have no freedom. He will have to march down the road to the end of time.
One must have a sense of freedom to judge his own actions and freedom from the effects of the actions of others. Where can this best be found but in the rural communities where there is freedom from the actions of one's neighbours. Above all, in rural life there is freedom to acquire a sense of co-operation. There is freedom to build a community and to co-operate with one's neighbours. There is a sense of building a better community and country. As politicians, we have to do much more than just espouse a high quality of life in the political speeches we make from time to time. It must be our goal and objective to give more and more people the opportunity to enjoy a high quality of life.
This afternoon I have tried to spell out what is encompassed within a high quality of life. Many of these objectives are quite attainable for a person who lives in an area that is not too densely populated. The more we group ourselves together, the more the quality of life diminishes. This government is deliberately attempting to destroy the quality of life that many Canadians in our rural community enjoy.
I wholeheartedly support this motion. I do not think that the payment of $100 million will reverse all the intentions of this government. I hope the government is continually bombarded with the theme that they alone are responsibe for this 20 page document which they are attempting to sell to agricultural ministers across Canada. This 20 page document will bring about the ruination of one of the best ways of life we have enjoyed to date.
For these reasons I support the motion. I hope the $100 million can be paid out quickly to help farmers make the necessary adjustments and judge the programs which are to be brought forward. If farmers are not worried financially about tomorrow's bread and butter, they might have time in which to assess fairly bills such as C-244 and C-176, and reject-

Mr. Speaker, on rising I should like to emphasize once again that nobody in this House has a better appreciation of the importance of farming and of farm life than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), and I assure once again, not members opposite who either do not hear or do not choose to hear but the agriculture community generally that everything we do in this government is designed to improve the basic position of farmers generally.
We shall, of course, attempt to offer special help, to develop special measures such as adjustment programs for farmers who are in a situation different from one they would choose for themselves. We in this government have been working very hard on measures to improve the agricultural situation in the long term. We have done so with firm convictions about the underlying strength of our agricultural industry and in the firm belief that with farmers and the government working together we can find an improved place for agriculture in this country.
What have we found from members opposite in these circumstances? We have found the doom and gloom boys once again at work, going across this land trying to suggest evil motives on our part, putting the worst possible light on every situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURAL POLICIES-IMMEDIATE PAYMENT OF $100 MILLION TO WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
It will be up to us in the government and in this party, and up to many other people across this land to attempt to counteract this doom and gloom and depict what the real possibilities are in order that men may work their best, not in the spirit of hopelessness which hon. members opposite have tried to instil but in the spirit of facing difficulties realistically and trying to overcome them.
I am happy to note that in the prairie region there are many who are trying to lead farmers to understand that difficulties can be overcome. I think, for example, of the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association, I think of the rape-seed associations of Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Canadian association particularly, not to ignore some of the others. These organizations have in recent days again emphasized the importance of marketing and of what can be done with our productive acres in the western region if we go after world markets with vigorous determination and a conviction that we can as a result claim those markets and benefit from an evergrowing share of income for the prairie region. It is men like these whose help we shall need, not just in describing the programs we have put in place but to overcome the attempt by members opposite to spread gloom and despair.
I think hon. members can do no worse in relation to agriculture than continue this attempt in which they have persisted for so long. I could point to the tremendous efforts which have been engaged in recently to bring some order and sense into the quota system, to remove programs which biased the system in favour of one grain or another. I could point to the large sums of money made available for diversion programs, the forage incentive program, and so on; programs which are directed to helping prairie agriculture and which are justified because this industry is in real difficulty and farmers have real cash problems in trying to make adjustments which they themselves know to be desirable.
Opposition spokesmen have drawn no attention to such things as federal efforts to place more cash into the hands of farmers by emphasizing wheat sales in our total world program. We have placed important emphasis on market development. The $10 million a year we have committed to market development is designed as seed money to produce much greater sums in the future. It is a tremendously positive attitude in respect of what our agricultural acres can do and where the future of agriculture may lie.
My colleague the Minister of Agriculture has recited how grain producers in many countries are now or have been in serious difficulty in recent years. Canadian producers have shared those difficulties to the full. In recognition of this, the government of this country has stood ready to expend large sums on behalf of the farmer. Members opposite talk about the net income position in the grain industry and how low it is. They do not pay attention to the $300 million which went from the treasury essentially to the grain producing area in 1970-71 in a totality of programs which in 1964-65 produced for the farmer about $92 million, a change of $200 million in additional money put out for the grain industry in recognition of its difficulties.
They do not recognize the other market developments and efforts which have been so important in the over-all planning, the extensive credit facilities which in the crop year ended July 31 made possible the export of some 150 million bushels of wheat and flour. That is about one-third of the total exports for that period and, significantly, it represents approximately the amount by which our exports of wheat this year may be above what some experts said would be the amount Canada would be able to sell in the world market. The government has at the moment outstanding liabilities of approximately $300 million in respect of loans in support of the sale of wheat where the federal government stands as guarantor. Hon. members choose to ignore this important contribution, again. On the market development side, the most positive side, looking to the development of better markets and improved cash position for the farmer by the sale of his own goods no matter what the treasury may do in relation to the farmer, the bulk of his income over a long period of time comes from the proceeds of sale of his own products and this is where the emphasis must be.

June 8, 1971

234.3	million bushels. In the case of Durum, exports were 33.7 million bushels compared with 14.9 million. In the case of oats, exports were 10.2 million bushels compared with 1.4 million bushels the previous year. In the case of barley exports were 135.6 million bushels compared with
49.3	million bushels. This 135.6 million bushels compares with the all-time previous record for an entire crop year of approximately 122 million bushels.

Hon. members say I should tell it to the farmers. Let me tell them other people in this country recognize that the $300 million which was paid out by the treasury is a significant amount of money, even if hon. members opposite do not appreciate it.
In the serious difficulties encountered in 1968-69 and 1969-70 the cash advance payments program was available and provided interest-free money to farmers to tide them over their difficulties. As a result, by the end of the last crop year a total of 122,110 cash advances had been taken for the year, for a total of $272,777,316. I should like to remind hon. members of the importance of this program to the extent that interest-free money is provided to farmers to tide them over the limited cash flow they experienced in the area of grain shipments.
I should like to illustrate how things are different this year. As of June 4, which will be approximately the end of the period for this year for cash advances, 51,353 cash advances have been taken. This compares with the previ-
Suggested Payment to Western Farmers ous year when 122,110 farmers took cash advances. The 51,353 taken this year represent a total of $91,105,330.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Now that all the preliminaries are over, Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill to outline why the

June 8, 1971

government wishes to establish and how it intends to operate the Canada Development Corporation. I have slowly and reluctantly come to the conclusion that this corporation will be the most costly fiasco which ever has been jammed down the throat of the Canadian people.
I am very disappointed this is the case because originally, before the government actually presented its bill, I had become convinced that this would offer an excellent potential for enabling Canadians to own and control more of their development. I believed that there were excellent possibilities presented for persuading Canadians, who do not now invest their savings in the stock market because they are unfamiliar with how it operates and therefore unwilling to trust their savings to it, to switch part of their savings to investment in the Canada Development Corporation.
However, because of the outline by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) concerning how the government intends the Canada Development Corporation should operate, I have reluctantly become convinced that the CDC will simply never get off the ground. I have come to this conclusion because of the method outlined by the Minister of Finance for raising the capital with which the corporation will operate. As we know, the government plan is that the corporation will raise 90 per cent of its capital-that is, $1,080 million-by selling shares to the public. In order for this to be possible it is obvious that the public must be willing to buy these shares. If the public is to buy these shares, the people must be convinced that investing in the CDC is a more desirable way for them to invest their savings than the method they are now using.
Let us examine the potential areas from which this capital can be raised. Most of the savings in this country are invested in two broad fields. The first is the stock and bond market, either through individual issues or through mutual funds. The second is the broad field of life insurance, savings accounts and Canada Savings bonds. Those who have been investing in the stock and bond market, either in individual issues or through mutual funds, have a wide variety of issues from which to choose. They are able to assess the possibilities for future growth and future dividends from the reports which companies make available periodically for the information of the public.
These people are satisfied with the method they are now employing for investing their savings and believe they are playing their part in helping this country finance its development. It is very unlikely that any of these people will be inclined to switch their savings from this type of investment to investment in CDC shares. The group which offers the real potential for switching its savings from the present form of investment to investment in the CDC is the second category, which includes those who have been investing their savings in life insurance, savings accounts and Canada savings bonds.
The combined savings of this group approaches $1J billion a year. I am convinced this group could be persuaded to switch part of its savings to investment in the CDC if an appeal were made to the people in it to help their country own and control more of its development. I
Canada Development Corporation believe something in the order of half a billion dollars a year could be switched from this group. In order for these people to be persuaded to switch part of their present investment to investment in the Canada Development Corporation they must be guaranteed the same kind of security and return on investment they are now receiving, which is very real and very attractive to them. They will not switch until they are assured of receiving at least the same security and the same return on investment.
The Minister of Finance recently announced that no such guarantee either of security or return on investment will be made by the government. I have discussed this matter at great length with people in the investment community. These are the people through whom sales of Canada Development Corporation shares would have to be made. They are unanimous in their opinion that unless the government gives such a guarantee to the people there will be no investment by the public in CDC shares.
Why are they so sure this would be the case? They will tell you the people are aware of what happens to business operations which are controlled by the government. They know very well what happened to the 14 companies that were operated by the late CCF government in Saskatchewan in the forties. We all remember the very interesting description given a few years ago by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he rose in this House and told us in chapter and verse what happened to each of the 14 companies operated by the CCF government at that time. He outlined how long each company lasted under the government's direction and what the loss was to the people of Saskatchewan in each case.
Mr. Speaker, a former leader of the government of Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), was in the House at the time and all he could do was smile and sink a little lower in his seat as the right hon. member for Prince Albert continued to describe the fiasco for which the hon. member's government was responsible.
The people of Canada are also familiar with the operation of Quebec's General Development Corporation which came into existence in the mid-1960s. This General Development Corporation is exactly the same kind of corporation the government intends the CDC to be. It was brought into being as a means of enabling the people of Quebec to participate in the development of industry of their province. In the same way, this government claims the CDC will enable the people of Canada to participate in the development of the Canadian economy.
The people of the business community in particular, the people of Quebec in particular and the people of Canada generally are aware that the shares of the Quebec General Development Corporation were placed on the market at $10 each. That was the highest point those shares ever hit. They have been going down gradually and steadily ever since and today they are offered to the public at $3.50 a share, with no takers. The reason for the sad experience of that corporation is the same as

June 8, 1971
Canada Development Corporation the reason for the sad experience of government-operated business enterprises in Saskatchewan. That reason is two-fold. The first is government interference, and the second is lack of managerial ability.
Without a government guarantee of security of investment and a return on investment, the people of Canada will simply not participate in the financial operation of the Canada Development Corporation, and anybody who thinks they will is completely out of touch with the thinking of the business community and, in particular, of the investment community on whom the government would have to rely 100 per cent to market these shares to the Canadian people.
People in the investment community will tell you that they simply cannot sell CDC shares unless there is a guarantee of security and return on investment. The government think that by appealing to the nationalism of the Canadian people, particularly the group that has savings and has never invested in anything in the nature of development, and by appealing their patriotism, they will achieve their goal. People in the investment community will tell you that without them there would simply be no investment by the public.
It shows how far out of touch with the business community the Minister of Finance and this government are if they think that their pipe dream of selling unsecured CDC shares to the public could be made a reality. It simply could not. All you have to do is ask any person in the investment community if this is not so and he will tell you that of course it is. When you mention CDC shares to the investment community, people simply laugh and the few that do not laugh, cry because it has become a very sad and a very sick joke among them. It is simply too ridiculous for words.
Because of these facts, because of the interference by the government if this corporation becomes a reality, because they know that the public will not participate in the financing of the corporation, more than 20 top businessmen in this country who have been approached to take on the job of president of the CDC, at a salary which I am told is about $75,000 a year, have turned down the proposition. They have turned it down cold because they know that this corporation will be a failure and top-flight businessmen do not like to be associated with failures.
That is why, also, the very large number of businessmen who have been approached to take on the job of general manager have turned it down. Businessmen do not like to be associated with failures and that is the reason this government will not be able to get a first-class businessman, a second-class or even a third-class businessman to take on the direction of the corporation. It will have to rely upon a political hack who has not been able to make a go of his own business and who would like to receive that large salary even for the few years that the corporation might be allowed to operate before it folds up like a $2 suitcase.
Finally, let us look at the use to which the corporation would put the $200 million of the taxpayers' money which the government intends to invest in the operations of the CDC. To get the answer let us ask ourselves first of all why, when the Canada Development Corporation lay dormant and unwanted for eight long years from the time it was first introduced by the then Minister of Finance, Hon. Walter Gordon, late last fall when the CDC legislation rated No. 74 on the government's list of legislative priorities suddenly it was elevated to No. 1. The bill was rushed into the House and now it is being put through in great haste.
The simple answer is that there is no economic reason for it; in fact, every economic reason is against it. It is a 100 per cent political reason. The reason is that the organizers of the Liberal Party suddenly saw in this proposal a first-class election gimmick. This corporation will be paraded on every Liberal platform in the country as a means by which anything that the people in the riding wish to take place in a business way will be promoted and accomplished. The CDC will be promised on every Liberal platform as the means by which companies which appear likely to fall into foreign hands will be taken over. It will be put forward as the means by which any company which is faltering and looks as though it is going under due to bad management or obsolescence of plant or machinery will be taken over.
People are not interested in a product which is obsolescent. The people in the area will be assured that the CDC will take over these companies, will put them on their feet and will put in all the money needed to keep them operating. Then if the government should have the good luck-which would be bad luck for the rest of the country-to be re-elected, which we hope to heaven it never will-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, OBJECTS, POWERS, CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
-you can count on the IOUs being presented to the government, and the parade to Ottawa of people from the ridings requiring that the government make good its promises will be really something to see. The Minister of Finance will try to withstand the storm, he will try to put them off, but there will be tremendous political pressure brought to bear which will make it impossible to withstand most of the pressure, and ridings that could be lost the next time around will be looked after very well indeed. If this legislation goes through and the CDC becomes a reality, we will see this corporation operating the greatest number of flops that you have ever seen. They will be operating companies that would make the 14 companies which failed in Saskatchewan in the 1940s look like very profitable and successful operations.
The trouble with the Minister of Finance, the government and its socialistic advisers is that they do not realize that for a company to be a practical success it must be able to produce a product at a price and of a design and quality which appeals to the buying public of this country as well as to the export market, because

June 8, 1971

most Canadian companies rely upon making sales in the export market. To do that a company must be relatively close to the source of raw materials. It must have cheap power, it must have the proper technology and it must have a market that wants its product and is willing to pay for it at the price that is asked and with the quality and design that is offered.
Most of the socialistic planners believe that all one has to do is put up the bricks and mortar, get the machines in and name a manager and somehow or other the company will be a success. That is the reason government-controlled business operations always fail. The public of Canada knows this of publicly-owned corporations of this kind and that is why it will not touch the CDC's shares unless security and return on investment is guaranteed: they will not touch them with a ten-foot pole.
So, Mr. Speaker, we will have on our hands a corporation that I am convinced will be the greatest flop since the Edsel. The Edsel is coming down the assembly line at the present time, and in the near future when the government's majority jams it through the House and makes it a reality, as it will, it will be operating on a gas tank that is only 10 per cent full. There are no drivers willing to direct the operations of the corporation because no first-class or second-class businessmen are willing to take it on. They are making that very clear. More than 20 top businessmen have been approached and every one has turned it down cold. No one will touch it because they do not want to be associated with a colossal failure.
Like its predecessor in this country and other countries, after costing the taxpayers many millions of dollars this corporation will be withdrawn. This has been the case in many instances. That, Mr. Speaker, is why 1 and members of the official opposition intend to vote against this measure on third reading.

He used his office as minister for the good of the people of Canada and ran his department in an efficient manner. Surely that must put the lie to some of the statements he made this evening to the effect that a government corporation cannot be run efficiently. We can expect this kind of talk from Liberals who do not have faith in corporations or government and are cynical about what can be done in the public sector, but I had hoped for something more from a former Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The Canada Development Corporation bill before us is disappointing in the extreme. It is unimaginative and does not meet the challenge of the crisis in Canadian development. And we are in a crisis. We are facing a situation where we cannot find employment for our people. We have the highest level of unemployment in the western world and have not been able to meet this problem despite the fact that we have imported so much foreign capital that the country has virtually been taken over.
The hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) has been criss-crossing Canada pointing out the serious consequences of the policies pursued by the government. He fees that far too much money from outside Canada is going to natural resource industries which do not provide benefits to Canada, do not provide us with tax revenues and employment opportunities and will in the long run destroy the ability of this country to survive.
The public senses that this is a phony bill. There has been almost no interest in it in representations before the committee despite the wide circulation of invitations to groups to appear before the House of Commons committee to present their points of view. The Canada Development Corporation has been met with a great big yawn. That is the kind of reception the government's CDC bill deserves. It is a nothing.
This bill is based on the false and unworkable premise, Mr. Speaker, that it must be a profit-oriented corporation and that is the only way to handle it. We have many profit-making corporations in Canada, so why are we in the sad state in which we find ourselves? Why is our economy virtually wrecked by foreign ownership? It is not because of the absence of a profit motive. We find ourselves in this state today because we have concentrated exclusively on the short-term profit motive; there is such thing as long-term profit. We have concentrated on giving away our resources and we have invited people to come in and virtually do as they please with our economy.
It will take more than this corporation to meet the chalenge of our times, Mr. Speaker. The bill is immoral in the sense that it attempts to take what is now the common property of all Canadians and convert it to the ownership of a few people. Corporations like Polymer have consistently returned a profit to the Canadian taxpayer as have Northern Transportation and Eldorado. It is wrong to take them away from the Canadian people to
June 8, 1971

Canada Development Corporation
whom they now belong and turn them over to a relatively small group which has money to invest.
After all, Mr. Speaker, only about 7 per cent of the Canadian population invests in equities at the moment. Even if more invest in the future, we will still be left with probably no more than 10 per cent and certainly no more than 15 per cent. This means that the minority of Canadians will be taking over the assets of the majority, and there seems to be no reason for this. If there is any justification at all for the CDC as the government sees it, it should stand on its own without having to be sweetened by taking public property and throwing it into the pot.
When we look at this bill we ask ourselves why the government has brought in such an emasculated, anaemic and meaningless piece of legislation and we come to a number of conclusions. The first is that they have been desperately trying to get rid of Crown corporations. The success of Crown corporations like Polymer apparently has been an embarrassment to them. We think they failed to get rid of them in the past because of public pressure, but think they can do it now by establishing the CDC and throwing Crown corporations into that combination.
Another reason is the paucity of equities for Canadian investors. I pointed out in a previous speech that a study conducted at York University indicated that there was a great deal of money in Canada looking for equity investment and it just was not available. Instead of taking action that would have been more appropriate under circumstances of this kind, as suggested by a former Minister of Finance, and insisting that branch plants of international corporations make their shares available in the Canadian market-after all, there is a shortage of equities in this country because of the high degree of foreign ownership of our corporations-the government chose to take the common property of Canadians and say, "You can now invest in these companies." That does not change the problem of foreign ownership. Actually, it makes the situation worse because we shall now take wholly-owned Canadian corporations and put them into a corporation which we are not sure will remain wholly under Canadian control.
The third reason is, I think, an entirely political one. In this I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. The government has political reasons for introducing this bill. It has promised to introduce the Canada Development Corporation for eight years. The failure to introduce it became embarrassing, so much so that the government felt it had to do something. This bill is that something. The CDC will not perform any real function. It does not seem to serve any significant purpose. However, since it has been promised in many throne speeches the government has introduced it. They will go into the next election and say, "You wanted the CDC. There it is."
I am afraid that the Liberal party is in for a rude awakening. The public of Canada is far more sophisticated than that party thinks. The public will see through this kind of fraudulent approach. It will see that the corporation is a nothing, that it is not what it purports to be. What the Liberal party may think is a political asset for them may turn out to be the greatest liability they have been burdened with for a long time.
The government's concept of CDC almost totally ignores the much wider problems facing Canada. The terms of reference of the corporation are not designed to help regional development; on the contrary, they will work against regional development because the idea behind the corporation is that it shall be profit-oriented. It is to be set up in anticipation of profits, as has been said.
The clause stipulating that the corporation cannot invest in businesses with capitalization of less than $1 million will work against the possibility of its becoming involved in regional development. The terms of reference of the corporation are the same as those governing companies in the private sector, and the private sector has failed miserably to meet the challenge of providing opportunities for Canadians wherever they may live in this country. The CDC will do nothing to come to grips with these disadvantages.
Instead of pouring millions and millions of dollars into regional development programs in the fond hope that private investment will somehow find its way to the underdeveloped parts of Canada and help in some undefined way, it would have been better if the money had been put into a development corporation which could have been established to bring about positive development. Such a corporation could have introduced a plan, in co-operation with the provinces, for the economic development of the underdeveloped parts of Canada. In that way we could bring proper development to those parts of the country which need industry and development.
The returns on the millions and millions of dollars being poured into the government's regional program are uncertain. On the other hand, by putting this money into a true development corporation we could do a great deal more and we could do it with the certainty that the money would be well spent and the results would be beneficial for areas which we are seeking to help. The government's regional development program is under an enormous cloud. It has become apparent that despite the department's vast expenditures almost no good has been done in the areas it has tried to help. A much better way of helping must be found if we sue to solve the problem of regional development.
The CDC, as the government sees it, is to be entirely a short-term proposition. It is to take short-term profits but is not to be concerned with the long-term interests of the country. There is a long-term interest, if I may use that phrase, Mr. Speaker, which needs to be met in this country. For instance, one of our great problems is that we need to rationalize our industry. Foreign investors have foisted an inefficient industrial structure on this country. I want to make it clear that this has not happened merely because investors have been foreign.

June 8, 1971

Some foreign investment can be advantageous. Most foreign investment in this country, particularly in the manufacturing sector, has been of a kind to benefit the international corporation which is investing. Much of it has not benefited us because foreign corporations did not set up industries which were indigenous to Canada and would have made sense in the Canadian economy. Actually, they set up a Dinky toy representation in this country of the American economy. They foisted on this country a miniature replica of the industrial pattern of the United States. Although that pattern may make sense in the United States, it does not make sense in this country. We may have modern plants; however, because they are not specialized and because many of them duplicate the activities of competitors, much of their production in Canada has proved uneconomical.
1 think everyone acknowledges that there is need for an intelligent rationalization of our industry. Although the terms of reference of CDC talk about rationalization, they hamstring the corporation with the basest of motives and the narrowest of objectives. Therefore, the kind of rationalization which ought to take place will not take place. That ought to be a prime function of a development corporation of any kind.
Another of our social and economic objectives has to do with the fair distribution of wealth in this country. However, instead of more widely distributing the ownership and the wealth of Canada we are narrowing that ownership, under this bill, to shareholders of CDC only. As I said earlier, we are taking corporations like Polymer which belong to all Canadians and putting them into the CDC. Thus, we are taking away ownership opportunities for Canadians and concentrating wealth in the hands of those who can invest in the CDC. Surely this is a retrograde step. We ought to be moving in the other direction and ensuring much wider ownership of our resources through the public sector so that all our people could participate in the investment, instead of narrowing the field by taking companies out of the public sector and putting them into the private sector.
If it is not intended that CDC shall come to grips with the question of foreign ownership and the government has carefully reminded us that it does not intend the corporation to do that, then what is the point of it? If it is not to come to grips with foreign ownership, why do we need it? The government says that other government policies are to tackle that problem. We have not seen any evidence of those other policies and in light of experience such statements must be treated with a great deal of suspicion. If there are such other policies, we had the right to be made aware of them before the CDC legislation was brought down, and the terms of reference for setting up CDC ought to have meshed with the aims of such policies instead of being in their present form. We do not know what those policies will be. We do not know what tax policies will be introduced. We do not know what the government's foreign ownership policies will be. We do not know what the policies relating to competition will be.
Surely the kind of development corporation required would depend to a great extent on government policies. It
Canada Development Corporation has been our view that CDC should be an instrument of government policy. Instead, CDC as presented to the House is to operate in the private sector. It is to act on its own, to follow the profit motive, and so on. There will be no guarantee that CDC will consider the public interest to a greater extent than any other corporation in the private sector.
The concept of a Canadian development corporation is particularly important to the New Democratic Party. After all, long before the government talked about this corporation our founding convention had dealt with the idea of such a development corporation. We felt it most important that there be such a corporation in Canada. It is for that reason our disappointment is so keen respecting what we have been presented with in this bill. It is also for that reason that we moved a large number of amendments, as it turned out in a vain attempt to change the bill in a way that would make it more acceptable and better adapted to serve the interests of the Canadian people. Every one of those amendments was turned down. It leaves us no choice but to vote against what my leader has called this emasculated version of a Canada development corporation. This is not a Canada development corporation in the sense that we wanted it to be. It is a name, and only a name. For that reason we cannot support the measure.
When we asked the government why the bill was presented in this form instead of a more flexible form that would be more responsive to Parliament and the Canadian people, we were told it was just a philosophical difference between our party and their party and that we see things differently. They did not even have the courtesy to make their arguments to show philosophically why their point of view was valid. They never even attempted to defend it; they simply dismissed our point of view as an ideological difference.
A study of other development corporations was put before the members of the committee. The study showed that no development corporation in any country had been set up in the form of the Canada Development Corporation. In other words, the government has not learned anything from what has gone on in the rest of the world or from their examination of the Canadian economy. There is hardly a country in the world that has not at one time or another actively intervened in its economy. This is even true of the United States which has the greatest hang-ups about government intervention in the economy. In each case they have intervened for different reasons. In Canada there is a most compelling reason why the government must play a more active role in the economy. The reason is that private entrepreneurship has failed the nation. We are in our present state because private entrepreneurs have failed us. That failure must be compensated by public enterprise. It is for this reason that we feel the Canada Development Corporation is of such importance.
It is always sad to participate in a committee hearing when the captains of Canadian industry turn out to be the strongest supporters for continuing foreign owner-

ship. People come before the committee, the representatives of the public, and say they do not want laws against foreign ownership. Their reasons are quite simple and clear. Laws of that type would restrict the opportunities to sell to a wider group of people and might restrict their profits. It is this mentality, coupled with the mentality of continentalist thinking and a government that has given us the highest degree of foreign ownership in Canada, that has made Canadians enormously insecure about their future and their ability to survive this kind of intrusion.
As I listened to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings I could not help wondering what the founder and first leader of his party would have thought of his speech. After all, Canada was built by public enterprise. The Conservative party more than any other party should be aware of this. This country was opened up by public, not private, enterprise. The Prairies were opened up by building the railroads. They were built at enormous expense to the public and tremendous involvement on the part of the government. Ontario Hydro was established by a Conservative government because it felt that businessmen could not function and would not be able to produce efficiently unless there were cheap power. This was not established by Socialists, although perhaps the reasons were socialistic. It was established because businessmen could not develop the industrial potential of Ontario unless cheap power were available. There was no reluctance at that time to bring about this kind of intrusion in the private sector.
Education, which is the infrastructure and backbone of any industrialized nation, is in the public sector. Even our culture is being preserved by the CBC and various grants and assistance to the arts in Canada. If it had not been done in the public sector it would not have been done at all. We would not have anything in Canada but American radio, television, newspapers and books. Banking started out as a private corporation in which all the banks participated after a great debate. After trying to operate in this way for a short time, in 1932, I think it was, it eventually became part of the operation of government. Today we can be proud of the Bank of Canada that we have. We are not proud of all its recent decisions, but on the whole the Bank of Canada is a wise institution. It is under public operation.
Those things in which Canada can take the greatest pride are under public operation, such as health, hospitals and the Canada Pension Plan. I have spoken to Americans who have visited Canada and seen what we have done in these areas. They envy the progressiveness of our public corporations and what they accomplish. I see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is in the chamber. We are sometimes very unhappy about our railroad system in Canada. There is a great deal that is wrong with the policies of our railroads. However, when you compare the railroads in Canada with those in a country such as the United States, our railroads stand out in startling contrast, particularly when we recognize the tremendous difficulty of transportation in this country.
Our air transport system is infinitely superior. The Americans are talking about doing some of the things

which we did a long time ago. Instead of spinning off another company and injecting CP Air, it would have been much better to have made this the prerogative of Air Canada, a Crown corporation. This does not only apply to Canada. In Great Britain, Chamberlain and Birmingham were not Socialists, yet many civil matters in the public sector had to be handled in a public manner. They were not reluctant to do so. Churchill, who would not like to have been called a Socialist, was responsible for bringing the railroads under public ownership. The telegraph operations came under public ownership at the time of Gladstone. I could go on. In the United States, people like Lincoln Steffens pointed out that you could not get rid of corruption in the public utilities until they came under public ownership.
