maintopic: HEALTH-INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL
HEALTH-INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the minister in the House last week whether consideration was being given to setting up a national council of health to correlate the various facets of research. As the situation is now, the ground is continually shifting as provincial and federal governments argue about who shall pay for the nation's health needs. Meanwhile, those in charge of medical education live a hand-to-mouth existence. The federal government brought in medicare. They based it on the findings of the Hall commission report which recommended that doctors, drugs and hospital beds must be available for all regardless of economic status. The report stressed that an immediate, all-out effort should be undertaken to increase the number of medical schools in order to train the increased number of doctors who would be required. This, of course, meant that money was needed, so the government set up what was called a health resources fund. It was established to help the province provide new schools, new equipment, scientist-teachers and the doctors required for research teaching and medical care.
What happened, Mr. Speaker? One of the first acts of the government was to cut back on the money it had promised and agreed to provide the health resources fund. It is interesting to note that the present Deputy Minister of Health, Dr. LeClair, who has had a good deal of experience as dean of the medical school at the University of Sherbrooke and received training at the Mayo Clinic, one of the outstanding clinics in the world, is quoted as saying:
Research and medical education is not something you pump for two or three years and then let the pump go dry.
It just does not work in that way; there has to be a steady increase in education on which you can count. I could quote other deans of medical schools in Canada who have expressed similar opinions to the effect that long-term planning is an essential of any health measure as well as short-term projects. Many of these projects were left unfinished when the health resources fund was cut. Incomplete buildings were left for the provinces to finish or to he as a stark monument to the folly of government policies. The result has not only been a slowdown in the training of doctors but the quality of teacher-scientists has diminished. The priority of equipping and training doctors has been seriously impaired.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, we have people today who have no doctor. Entire areas are without medical care. At overworked outpatient departments of hospitals people wait, often for hours, for an overworked doctor to treat them. The doctor image is being destroyed because of lack of time for proper communication and owing to the
swamping of the doctor's time to fill in forms and papers, and red tape of this kind.
Drug care was to be a supplement to medicare so that the poor patient of limited resources would not only have his doctor's bill paid but also his drugs. Not a thing has been done in this regard. I raised this question in the House on a motion and government speakers who replied were in total agreement in principle with the motion. But what has been done to implement it? Paramedical services have been neglected. The poor people still do not know who is going to pay their bills. Individual doctors who are doing research are denied funds for clinical research purposes. This, then, is the reason we need a Canadian council of health. We need to set down priorities that will be followed and which will obtain the maximum result for the taxpayers' dollars.
Dr. John C. Beck, physician and chief director of McGill University's clinic at Montreal's Royal Victoria Hospital, has stated that although seven years ago national goals were defined by the Hall commission report on health services there is still no national science policy for health. Dr. Beck stated that a national health policy would seem to be of the very highest priority when costs are escalating and taking 6 per cent of the gross national product, $7 billion.
Federal and provincial governments have not stated their policies or their plans for health services systems. They have not stated their policy on financial support for the training and necessary research for such systems. Instead, we have unco-ordinated expansion of facilities and excessively expensive arrangements for the delivery of health services, and the cost is much higher than it ought to be.
We have been unable to formulate and implement planned programs for developing health manpower, for recruiting staffs to the health science centres and for carrying out good scientific research. Dr. Hollenberg, professor and chairman of the University of Toronto school of medicine, states that Canadian medical scientists are experiencing considerable uncertainty over the national effort on medical research. There is a slowing rate of growth in the budget of the Medical Research Council of Canada-

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) stated in reply to the question of the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), we do not agree with the hon. member's premise that there is no national health science policy. Health science is the responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and he carries out this responsibility through his department and through the Medical Research Council. These bodies are continually co-operating on matters of science policy and, as a matter of interest, are at this time reviewing together the entire question of health science research. In addition, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and officials of his department co-operate closely with federal, provincial and municipal authorities and with universities and health science associations.

maintopic: HEALTH-ALLEGED USE OF STALLING TACTICS TO PREVENT ABORTION APPLICATION BEING DEALT WITH
HEALTH-ALLEGED USE OF STALLING TACTICS TO PREVENT ABORTION APPLICATION BEING DEALT WITH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to raise this matter again just when the Medical Association has registered its opinion that abortion is justified on non-medical social grounds. On May 20 I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) about a complaint by Dr. Byron Hyde, a general practitioner on the staff of the Riverside Hospital in Ottawa, that stalling tactics are being consistently used by those in charge of the hospital to prevent abortion cases from coming before their review board. I asked the minister if he would consult with the minister in charge of hospitals in Ontario to see what could be done about this dangerous and indefensible roadblock. The answer was silence, complete and unbroken silence.
I do not think this is good enough. The Minister of Justice is in charge of the Criminal Code which legalizes abortion where the life or health of the pregnant woman is in danger. The minister is fond of quoting the definition of "health" given by the World Health Organization:
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
Evidently certain hospitals like Riverside refuse to accept this definition when it is applied to abortion. They refuse to accept "social well-being" as an essential part of a woman's health; and they crack down on it so efficiently that women are obliged to leave their own doctor and shop around other hospitals in Ottawa or elsewhere, including the state of New York. Meanwhile the nine-month time clock keeps ticking away relentlessly.
Obviously no hospital is going to acknowledge that it is deliberately undermining the law of the land by openly
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
throwing up roadblocks in the way of legal abortions. But equally obviously, many hospitals like Riverside can organize their abortion committees effectively to prevent legal abortions. To quote Mr. Jackson Bryan, Riverside's administrator:
If there was any emergency, Dr. Hyde could have applied to the Civic or Grace Hospitals.
To quote Dr. Hyde:
The fact is, every unwanted pregnancy is an emergency. Can Mr. Bryan's statement mean anything other than that Riverside is not available for consideration of therapeutic abortions? ... The fact is, the Riverside Hospital, like many Ontario hospitals, takes the federal law and adds its own riders to make the law unworkable. The abortion law is part of the federal Criminal Code.
I am convinced that it is time now for the Minister of Justice to put an end to this chicken and egg war. If the Criminal Code is such that provincial hospital authorities can add riders to it to suit their own prejudices, let the minister meet with the appropriate provincial authorities to see that the law is applied equally to all citizens. Right now the abortion provisions are gambling with the lives of women who are so unfortunate as to live where hospital authorities are determined to flout the spirit of the law, if not its letter, to keep them out.
A few days ago Lore Perron, founder and president of ARCAL, the Association for the Repeal of Canadian Abortion Laws, showed reporters a copy of a letter dated March 20 to A. B. R. Lawrence, Ontario health minister. It pointed out that of six general hospitals in the Ottawa-Hull area three have no abortion committees because they are administered by religious organizations. And at the Riverside Hospital the chief and the assistant chief of obstetrics and gynecology oppose abortion because of their religious convictions, as do other members of the abortion committee. That letter said that for health reasons, mental and physical, they will not grant abortions, which leaves the Ottawa Civic Hospital carrying the load for at least four of the major hospitals.
Mrs. Perron made the very just and sensible comment that doctors obviously prejudiced against abortion should not be appointed to abortion committees. She also stated the following and I would like particularly to draw this to the attention of the minister:
Hospitals receiving public funds, whether or not they are being administered by religious organizations, should be instructed by the province that they must permit doctors who have privileges at a hospital to use its facilities.
This, of course, would permit Dr. Byron Hyde to perform an abortion on a patient at the Riverside Hospital even if the chief and the assistant of obstetrics and gynecology were opposed to the idea of abortion. As Dr. Hyde himself remarked:
Riverside Hospital physicians who support impediment of the federal law are remnants of another era, and they have their counterparts in hospitals across the land.
It is time for the Minister of Justice to assure himself and the rest of us that the law will be applied with even-handed justice.

June 8, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mr. Albert Bechard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, as the hon. lady very well knows, the provisions of the Criminal Code are in the first instance prohibitory insofar as abortion is concerned, and then provision is made for certain exceptions. The manner of qualifying for those exceptions is clearly set out in section 237 of the Criminal Code and is a matter which is entirely within the jurisdiction of the people named therein, who are the Minister of Health, the board of an approved or accredited hospital, a qualified medical practitioner and, if a hospital chooses to establish one, a therapeutic abortion committee. With respect to the practice in any particular hospital and the exact manner in which any application for abortion is processed by the people who are lawfully entitled to consider it, this is not a matter which should concern the Minister of Justice.

maintopic: BROADCASTING-POLICY ON ISSUANCE OF LICENCES TO AGENTS OF CROWN IN PROVINCES
BROADCASTING-POLICY ON ISSUANCE OF LICENCES TO AGENTS OF CROWN IN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am here tonight on the adjournment motion debate because of a few loose remarks by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). On Thursday June 3, as recorded at page 6324 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister if there was any change in federal policy prohibiting the issuance of broadcasting licences. Among other things, the Prime Minister said that there is no encroachment upon the policies of the federal government. Later, on June 7, and again in reply to a question to the Prime Minister on the proposed sale of the assets of National Cablevision Limited to a consortium of interests, the Prime Minister said as recorded at page 6412 of Hansard:
I understand that the purchase was not by any government, but mainly by insurance companies. Therefore it is a private purchase.
Mr. Speaker, it may be all right for the Prime Minister to go to Russia and issue either naive or simplistic statements about the federal institution in Canada or about the status of Ukrainians in Canada, but when it comes to a question as basic as federal power in broadcasting, for example the issuance of broadcasting licences, I suggest it is time he should be held accountable for his words.
A quick review of some of the regulations and of the legislation of the Prime Minister's government would show, first, that the issuance of broadcasting licences is an encroachment on federal policy and, second, that it is not a private matter, a matter of a sale between insurance companies, because the proposal filed on May 31 before the CRTC is for the sale of controlling interests of National Cablevision Limited to, among others, Caisse de Depot et Placement du Quebec, the Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund. The controlling interests of the Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund amount to 30 per cent, which under section 29 of chapter 23 of the Statutes of Quebec of 1965 is the maximum that the fund can hold in any company, and that is the controlling interest in the proposed application. Section 4 reads:
The fund shall be an agent of the Crown in right of the province.
Yet the Prime Minister stands in this House and says that this is a private matter and is not an encroachment on federal policy. A directive of his government issued on June 4, 1970, pursuant to section 27 of the Broadcasting Act says, among other things:
The Canadian Radio-Television Comission is hereby directed that, on and after the 4th day of June, 1970, broadcasting licences may not be issued-
The following people are named. Section 2(a) reads;
Her Majesty in right of any province and agents of Her Majesty in right of any province-
Section 3 reads:
For the purposes of this direction, "agents of Her Majesty in right of any province" means any agents of Her Majesty in such right and includes a municipal or public body empowered to perform a function of government in a province or any corporation empowered to perform a function or duty on behalf of Her Majesty in such right.
Therefore, I submit that it is clear, on the face of the Prime Minister's directive issued by his own cabinet pursuant to the Broadcasting Act, that no licence can be issued under the present broadcasting policy to an agent in right of a province, which is what the Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund is, pursuant to section 4.
My question to the Prime Minister was whether there has been or will be a change in federal policy. He pretended to be frivolous or facetious and suggested that there was not to be any change. Later he said it was a private matter. When there are serious constitutional discussions in Victoria on the shape and size which Canada is to take as we move into the 1970s, I suggest that it is contempt of Parliament for the Prime Minister to treat such a serious matter in this frivolous way.
It may be all right for the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who is charged with the responsibility of answering for the CRTC to this House, to say that he is joyful now that the minister responsible for broadcasting in the province of Quebec has worked out a particular deal with the federal authorities so that the impasse or dispute on cablevision can be resolved, and I am not suggesting that it may not be an adequate and proper method by which the federal and provincial governments can work out their difficulties; but I suggest in all seriousness that it is close to contempt of Parliament to say that there is not to be a change in broadcasting policy.
If the policy on June 4, 1970, had any application or relevance, then there has to be consistency with what has been suggested by the Prime Minister. If there is to be a change, let the government admit it. If there is not, then the CRTC should not even be charged with considering the application which it has on file.
